doc.title: Mrs. Mary Lucy Hamill O'Kelly Interview, 1958-05-04

title: Her background and first impressions of jazz as embroidered tunes
summary: She gives her birth in 1876 in Mississippi, marriage and move to New Orleans in 1909. She saw jazz as black musicians' embellishment of regular tunes, and recalls Piron's band and a Halfway House band the teenagers listened to from parked cars.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Well, this is Mrs. Mary Lucy Hamer O'Carrie. Born Mary Lucy Hamer in 1876 at Fixford, Mississippi. Lived after my marriage in 1900 at Ashwood, Louisiana, on the plantations that my husband came to New Orleans in 1909. Built a home there and lived in New Orleans until 1940. When I came to Paschus Jan to leave it. I was going home there. And I can't remember when. I first viewed jazz as being jazz. I just thought it was sort of embroidery that the niggers put on tunes that they played. They were not embedded as jazz tunes except the one I remember was the St. Louis Blues. They, these nigger bands would take any regular tune and jazz it up. They'd add little extra notes and quavers and trills and runs and syncopation and make the thing sound entirely different. For a long time we just thought it was something that they all took to naturally because I never heard any neighbor sing a tune exactly as it was written by white people. They always added some little trimming to it. They, uh, let's see, one band I remember in New Orleans was Piron's band. Played very well. There were numbers of smaller bands that played down, down we called the French Quarter and the French Quarter. Do you remember the Crossman's Day of the Rings? No, that was around 1915 I should say. And there was one very good band, I think it was after it was called the Dixie Lane Band, the Dixie Lane Band, which was, uh, downtown on the road from, let's see, from, where was it? Well, it was called the Halfway House. People who live in New Orleans would know more about the Niles because I don't remember. But I remember that our young people, teenagers, were not allowed to go to this nightclub at Halfway House, but they used to drive up near it and park and sit in the cars listening to this band. They all thought it was perfectly wonderful.
